While being a mad-dog veteran of the sequel title, Battlefront 2005 on PS2, I didn't actually own a copy of the game that started it all until years later. I've played 2004 far less than '05.

Star Wars battlefront 2004 is a good game nevertheless, and still a solid title today if you ask me. It has mechanics and features that 2005 dropped in favor of streamlining or balancing, like being able to go prone.
Infinite left and right strafe rolling with no stamina cooldown, Or the Sniper class having a hipfire crosshair, effectively making it the best run and gun class.

If you don't care about hero play and want specialist classes unlocked from the start of the match, this is the game for you.  The Imperial "Dark Trooper" for example is better than his cousin from 2005, that electricity gun sucks, and this game's dark trooper gets a shotgun, a real mans weapon. Jetpack in and blow people away. Balance-wise this game isn't as fair compared to 2005, but I think that's what makes it fun and worth playing, both titles have their own little mechanics and it keeps them distinct from one another.

There are land warfare maps that actually include aircraft, something absent from the sequel. (Can only fly ships in space battles.) And the classes per team are more unique, sometimes to your benefit and sometimes not. And despite some locations from the films being in both games, the maps you get from those locations are often wildly different, so its not like SWBF 2005 is a direct replacement for SWBF 2004.

Multiplayer was brought back online after the death of Gamespy by Disney. And the game occasionally gets bugfixes and updates by the new development team. 

Online matches work, and I know for a fact Peer-to-Peer matches work in this title from personal experience, thanks to the one random who joined my lobby two years ago, you da man.

I think the mechanics not brought over into 2005 from this game are the reason you should play 2004, It's just different enough and still has the same fun gameplay loop of its more popular younger brother.

PS, name a player profile "Jub Jub" to enable tiny mode in singleplayer, everyone's the size of a Jawa, its great.

And holy mother of Christ, this thing delivered like nothing else. Games lived up to the hype back then. What was radical was that it came in a smaller box, 13.5cm wide, 3cm fat and 19cm tall. It wasn't a big fat massive box like JKA  or Diablo. Those big fat box days were over for good now with the new streamlined design. 3 whole CDs were needed to install it. Disc 1 was indeed the play disc (who would have guessed lol).

I've only had a handful of minutes on this compared to what I had as a kid, but I just wanted to kinda "remind" people what they are paying for.
This is actually kinda hard compared to Battlefront 2 Classic. I was a little shocked by it considering how much FPS I've played since then and the difficulties I've grown to work with. It's hard to play anything BUT the basic soldier, sniper, and on some maps the pilots. But each class has their uses and points. The reason why I say class selection lends itself to difficulty is the fact you'll have (example) the shock trooper/rocket class where you're given well... a launcher, a peashooter, some mines and the duty of being the dedicated "kill one tank (hopefully)" role. Obviously if you make it to some ammunition this isn't a problem but it doesn't have the punch or grit to lend itself a viable for solo play. Upon a recent touch through Galactic Conquest, if you want this class to perform well, you need to get the sabotage bonus. 

The controls still feel really good after all of these years and there's a big amount of charm to this game into tickling your imagination compared to the recent ones. This isn't a bash to EA but this is something that I feel gives this game its selling point, this is you making a fantasy from the most of what you got. Before all the lore, tv shows, games, films etc, this was the gaming community's way of living out a mental fantasy and it's the best approach to have when playing this. If Darth Revan is treated as a self insert, then this is your military self insert into the story of the Clone Wars and Galactic Civil War. 
Just make a little head cannon of what you're doing and you'll enjoy it immensely. "Capturing this ancient Naboo statue will serve as a landing point for the invasion" or "This fight in the Dune Sea isn't a hamfisted attempt to cram every Star Warsy thing in here, this is Uncle Owens cousin's place...named Phil".

Look we were all weird kids... But that's the point and I hope other Star Wars fans feel this way with EABF2 on missions like Hoth or the beach invasion during CoOp. Not every game needed to be a one-to-one recreation of a battle and I applaud Pandemic and even EA when they shook off these concepts with Yavin 4 and Rhen Var.

There's a huge lack in modes compared to the second, lack of classes, but at least you can pilot a jankey Tie Fighter or X-Wing on some maps on the planet's surface and it's not restricted to a battlephase either. No hereos either. God, I remember writing a letter to the devs when I played my first 20 hours with my dad about adding heroes to the sequel. I think I even begged for a "cheat code" to have it as an unlock lol. 

Anyways nostalgia aside, it's a little harder than what I remember, very very bare bones, and the campaign is nothing short but "white bread". But this is essential to any fan's collection, it's a stepping stone, and to me replaying it has been humbling to see how far we've come to games and it helped me appreciate the most recent Battlefront by EA more in terms of really hammering home the thrill of massive battles and desperate charges to gain a "high ground". Don't lie, heavy class clones with the main canon ability is still just as cool as Commander Thorn.
It's still a joy to play and even though I have about an hour or into this, you can expect me to pop it open once in a while to remind myself to be a humble gamer, appreciate where my dad sucked me into the world of Playstation 2 game nights with Bagel Bites and rainy afternoons. It's a nostalgia trip.

Also, I've updated the review for some minor things I wanted to add and as I typed this at arguably a falling out as a Star Wars fan, I type this with a newfond appreciation of "new things". That doesn't mean I'm apologizing the Sequels or thinking Disney rolling into GCW content again will "fix" anything. It just means that, especially looking back what I said about headcanons and self inserts, we as a community champion this. Look at the costuming communities, lightsaber builders, and how Lego Star Wars offered customs, how people ramble over what lightsaber form they do, where they'd like to live in the universe, etc. etc.

I feel as a community we think too heavily on the canon versus a blossoming world of potential. With the lack of show from KOTOR in the Playstation show today 5/24, I think we need to continue to write our own personal narratives and not get caught up in the guff of it. It's a galaxy's worth of cultures, narratives, and possibilities, don't limit yourself because it's not canonized or something isn't to your liking.

Happy Gaming and continue to champion your inner kid.

This game is aaaahhh how do you say....a blast from the past.

"You can never go wrong with the classics", as the old saying goes. Yes this game is almost 20 years old at the time of this review. Yes the graphic did not age well. Yes the game mechanics did not age well. But dammit, this game is from the time of when games where made with passion, blood, sweat, and tears and limited budgets. This was the golden age of gaming in my opinion. While this might not be for everyone, this is definitely one for you old school Star War fans.

This game is really decent in comparison to the sequel Star Wars Battlefront 2 (Classic, 2005). Of course, it is missing several things that the sequel has, but the sequel is missing several things that this game has as well. One example being how you can shoot the trees on Yavin IV and birds will fly out of them. The sequel doesn't have that. Or you could play certain maps that do not exist in the sequel, such as Bespin or Rhen Var.

On top of that, this game has really good modding support. Now although this game is a bit.. dead.. when it comes to modding, I really do think that this game is far ahead of it's time in terms of that. The vanilla game is good, but it's like 1000x better with modding!

Now as for multiplayer, I've never really played multiplayer on this game so I don't have a lot to say about it. But I do know that it's just as fun as playing multiplayer in the second!

My only real complaint for this game is that it's not as fast-paced as the sequel, but it's not that bad. It's one of those things where you could get used to it. I used to play this game a lot on the Playstation 2 way back in the early 2010s and you could really feel how slower the game is in comparison to the sequel in terms of pacing. Of course, this is the PC version so it's obviously different than the PS2 version that I used to play.

So in summary: This game is good, almost as good if not better than the sequel in some aspects, and this game is very good in terms of modding. Of course it's a bit slower in pace but if that is okay with you, then this game is perfect!

195 hours later and I would recommend!

The debate when it comes to Star Wars Battlefront isn't whether or not you should buy it, it's *which* one do you buy? To answer that, I only really consider two options; SW:BF 2004 and SW:BF2 2005. The difference between the two being that 05 has more content but I find the content that is in BF 04 is generally more fun to play with. In this game you are a standout soldier in an army while in 05 you are *the* army. You'll sometimes die to stuff in 04 that you couldn't do much other than try to avoid whereas in 05 you get rewarded with very powerful heroes units to demolish the other team with after just a few kills. The maps in 04 are also on average better than 05, but they can all be modded into 05 so I would not take that in account when purchasing. As a final remark, the AI is somehow much better in this version. I've seen others say this online and I didn't think it would be true, but after playing for a while I have to agree. It may be a quirk in the way that this version interacts with the maps (whereas 05's might not), but the AI tends to create large centerpiece battles while still having units who find themselves on the fringes doing something (sniping or flanking). If you do pick the game up, make sure to use something like RivaTuner to lock your fps to 60 or even 30 because the game starts to break if you go too high.

Overall, BF2 2005 has a lot more content and more replay-ability value so, if you're looking for raw dollar to gameplay value, I'd go there, but this game also has a lot of fun quirks to bring to the table and I would definitely pick it up when you can.

[h1]Just like old times![/h1]

I was pleasantly surprised when I saw Classic Battlefront on the Steam store, the perfect surprise too for May the 4th be with you. Next to Halo 2, this is one of the first shooter games I played over a decade ago, so it holds a special place in my heart for all the hours I spent playing Classic Battlefront.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

To simplify Battlefront, it's a Star Wars version of Battlefield, that is surprisingly fun; this is why we love it. Gameplay in Battlefront is conquest-based which can either take place in the Clone Wars or the Galactic Civil War. Each faction has a finite amount of reinforcements, 250 soldiers about, and each is given control of a set number of command posts in a given level. If you hold more command posts than your enemy, they will bleed respawn tickets and vise versa. The object is to either eliminate enemy forces or capture and hold all command posts simultaneously for 20 seconds. Several ground and air vehicles are available on the battlefront. Air to ground combat and more than 25 different vehicles in the game, in either a third-person perspective, or a view from the interior of the vehicle which is really unique and immersive. Every faction has an announcer that gives you updates on the battle "We've gained control of a command post!" "Separatist forces have lost the Spire!"
My favorite gimmick of Battlefront is that some maps have indigenous forces. These can be neutral to both factions, such as Jawas, hostile to one faction, such as Wookies or Gungans, or hostile to both factions, like the Tusken Raiders on Tatooine's Dune Sea who would attack everybody.
The game also runs like smooth butter on PC.

[h1]Story[/h1]

Not too much to say here, The single player just follows the main battles seen in the films. You will better understand each and every battle if you have seen the movies, but they did put in various clips and from said movies and mission briefing before each battle so the player better understands what's at stake, even if they haven't seen any of the movies. There are some battles thrown in that didn't take place in any of the movies, but I'm okay with that because it adds maps and more gamplay opportunity I.E The Separatists never attacked Kamino in the movies (but in an episode of the animated TV show). There's even a battlefront on a planet we never even hear or see in the movies, Rhen Var.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

To summarize, STAR WARS Battlefront (Classic, 2004) was more or less an experiment that was surprisingly fun, and layed the foundation for this great series, it innovated in all the right places, and most importantly, the game offered the immersion of being a soldier in the greatest battles of the Star Wars Universe

My final rating for STAR WARS™ Battlefront (Classic, 2004) is a 10/10. Pick this game up without hesitation, especially during a sale; this is a true classic. Thanks for reading my review, and I will see you on the next one.

This review is going to be a little biased since Star Wars Battlefront is perhaps the first game I ever played  on a near-religious level back in the day when my gaming addiction was in its infancy - we're going back nearly twenty years here, when I saw my dad playing this game on the family computer. Looking back, it was certainly a day of prophecy. Before the dark times. Before the Empire. Anyway, this game, brought to us by the blessed developers at Pandemic Studios in 2004, is not only one of the best Star Wars games out there, but is a fantastic experience in its own right. I mean, simple things like 'We've captured a command post' or 'Victory is imminent!' are iconic for a reason.
 
This game grabs you by the hand and truly does take you to a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, where you are handed a rifle and expected to partake in some of the fiercest conflicts of the Clone Wars or perhaps the Galactic Civil War, in which you assume the role of just another statistic in the galactic database, or (if you're a good enough player) become a rogue legend that can't be killed by anyone or anything as you take command post after command post in a frenzied streak of sci-fi badassery. 

If I sound a bit dramatic about it, please remember that this game was my go-to time-killer; whether it was right after a long day at school or just another 8am on a Saturday. It's really a shame there aren't more games with this perfectly refined gameplay; intricate enough to be infinitely interesting and different every time, yet also simplified to the point where anyone can jump in and never feel out of place  amongst your computer-controlled teammates that you'll fight and die alongside. 

Unlike Battlefront II (which is somehow inferior in my humble opinion) we are granted vehicles capable of flight on some maps, which is such a satisfying mechanic that I'm not really able to articulate why I like it as much as I do. Hop in and blow an X-Wing or a Vulture droid out of the sky in an epic Star Wars dogfight, reign terror on the ant-like infantry down below, or even invent your own super cool strike team like something straight out of one of these movies as you land behind enemy lines and snatch those command posts up to confuse and dominate your pitiful enemy. I tell you, this game makes me feel like Napoleon Bonaparte or something as I plan my attacks and conquer the battlefield in a series of lightning-fast strategic moves that crush the opposition in a spectacular display of Star Wars-esque action and heroism. In my honest opinion, I can't think of many games that capture such feats of adventure in an otherwise seemingly basic shoot-'em-up style, like this game here.

The class selections are very cool as well, especially for the sleek Imperials or the nicely colour-coded Clone troopers. They really did think of everything for this game - you can be a sniper, you can fly, you can blow up giant Star Wars vehicles with your demolitions - even play as wookiees and the frankly overpowered droidekas. Mix that with really engaging and respectably-detailed Star Wars locations and you have a seriously cool game that I'm sure was one hell of a love letter to fans back when it launched. The soundtrack, while it can be a little repetitive, seems to know exactly when to play too. And let's face it: it's Star Wars music. That stuff is borderline therapeutic. 
 
If we're going to talk the negatives, and it is important that we do, then I'll begin by pointing out that while the game's gameplay is very, very fun, the supposed campaign is a blatant afterthought full of recycled maps and non-existent objectives other than 'win'. There really isn't anything to these so-called missions other than admittedly nostalgic snippets from the films themselves. Ignoring campaign, the galactic conquest mode is perhaps a little bit more interesting, yes, but it sure does get old quick, and you're essentially just getting the same experience as you would with instant action mode. 

Multiplayer is also completely devoid of players, but this should be expected seeing as there has indeed been quite a bit of water under the bridge since this was the hot new game in town. But even as a kid all I wanted to do was play offline against the dumb-headed bots, which is a testament to the enjoyment of the game. And yes, while they are indeed quite simplistic (which can tend to be very unfortunate when you find yourself depending on these idiot teammates now and again) they actually are quite threatening when they want to be, especially on hard difficulty. The game is also pretty rigged at certain times as well, which ain't too sporting. Seriously, I will pay you a thousand Republic credits if you can beat Kashyyyk: Islands on hard difficulty playing as the Empire. Good luck, youngling.
 
The so-called 'instant action heroes' (Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, Mace Windu, Darth Tyranus) are designed as if the game developers put a keyboard in front of their young children and told them to play. They're so ridiculously out-of-place that I've seen the bots just run on by them as though embarrassed to even be fighting with them. Yeah, they suck... although it never gets old firing a rocket launcher under Vader's feet to witness him free-fall off the edge of a huge cliff down to his death. Now THAT'LL make you feel like a true hero for the Alliance.

Perhaps most important overall (and maybe even the reason you're reading this review) is the million-dollar question: is this game still worth it in 2023? The answer is a big yes, especially if you enjoy Star Wars (...and especially if you HATE modern Star Wars, bleh). It's honestly quite impressive how a game this old has held up so nicely. Okay, yes, when too many enemies are on-screen they become deformed hunchbacks which takes you out of it a little, and playing in first-person dates the game even further, but it is still a very pretty game. Definitely play in third-person, though. Playing on max settings shouldn't be an issue for any respectable P.C gamer in this decade, and it's a bonus that the characters/vehicles/ships all control very nicely. 

I want to close this review by reminding you that the new Star Wars Battlefront games are just sad imitations of two genuinely inspired games, and for that reason you really can't go wrong buying this. But you knew that already, right? There's no in-game transactions (or, ahem, rampant political correctness) to be found here! No, sir! 

So, pick a class, load up and remember: wE mUsT dEsTroY thA sHiElD gEnuRaTuH!

[h1]They're losing reinforcements![/h1]
[i]Star Wars[/i], like it or not, is a global phenomenon. It's attracted legions of fans (myself included) across pretty much every conceivable age, inspiring thousands upon thousands of people. It is, and will continue to be, a timeless story. Despite the divisive fanbase, which has split [i]Star Wars[/i] into a fractured state, warring against each other, I am proud to be able to proclaim that I like pretty much all [i]Star Wars[/i]. Perhaps the only film that disagrees with me is [i]The Rise of Skywalker[/i] but honestly a huge part of me still enjoyed it. 

But I think that no matter what era of [i]Star Wars[/i] you like most - whether it be the Original Trilogy, the Prequel trilogy, the original Expanded Universe (my personal favourite!), the new trilogy, or some other part of it I haven't listed here (I could go on for a long time...) - you will love [i]Star Wars Battlefront[/i]. 

Have you ever wanted to be a squad leader, leading a group of Imperial Stormtroopers (only their aim could be so precise) into a Rebel temple on Yavin IV? Were you ever inspired by the vistas of Cloud City, and did you ever want to fly one of those little Cloud Cars? Are you fascinated with the designs of the Prequel-Era Clone Troopers and Droidekas? Have you ever wanted to be just one of the soldiers in [i]Star Wars[/i], and not one of the big important people? If you answered yes, I think [i]Battlefront[/i] is for you. 

Probably if you've made your way here already you already know you want this game. But I'll lay it out, just in case you don't know what's going on. It functions a lot like the [i]Battlefield[/i] games - choose your class of soldier, which ranges from standard assault rifle grunt to specialized tech engineers - and capture command posts around the map. But the [i]Star Wars[/i] flavour - the music, the sounds, the design, etc. - adds a huge amount to the game. Instead of boarding a military helicopter and firing boring old assault rifles, like you would in most games, you get to soar through the skies in a TIE Fighter and dodge lasers fired from one of the LAAT/I Clone gunships while hearing the satisfying pew-pew of your laser gun, or the sonic guns of the Geonosians. You throw EMP grenades to disable Droideka shields, or tie up AT-ATs with tow cables as they try to blow up the shield generator. 

Simply put, this game is a work of absolute nostalgic genius that plucks all the right [i]Star Wars[/i] heartstrings. The one "flaw" is that the game was released in 2004, which is one year before the release of [i]The Revenge of the Sith[/i]. So we only see Phase One Clone Troopers for instance, and there are of course no Resistance or First Order options for fighting. But honestly, you get your money's worth here. It has Steam multiplayer support, it has four different conquer the galaxy mini-campaigns and two other campaigns that follow the events of both wars (The Clone and Galactic Civil Wars), and an instant action map-select mode where you make your own war. You really can't go wrong if you are a [i]Star Wars[/i] fan. It should probably already be in your wishlist or your library. 
May the Force be with you!

This game? Pure nostalgia. But it’s more than that.

Yeah, it’s from 2004. The graphics are dated, the menus creak like an old PC case, and the AI still sometimes forgets how to shoot. But the feel of it? Still unbeatable. You drop into the middle of a chaotic battlefield — stormtroopers and rebels everywhere, tanks rolling through, starfighters dogfighting above your head — and for a second, it’s like you’re in Star Wars.

The class system is simple but satisfying. The maps are iconic: Hoth, Endor, Kamino — every one has that “just one more round” effect. You can switch from soldier to pilot, jump in a speeder, grab a turret — it’s controlled chaos. The kind of game where you go from capturing command posts to crashing a snowspeeder into an AT-AT because... why not?

Multiplayer is hit or miss these days (depends on community servers), but honestly? I don’t mind playing solo. Instant Action still slaps. It’s that old-school fun where it doesn’t take itself too seriously, but you still feel like a hero when you clutch a match with 10 reinforcements left.

If you played this back in the day, it’s like opening a time capsule. If you haven’t? Just know it’s a classic for a reason.

If you're torn between this, and Star Wars Battlefront 2 (2005), I recommend getting this one. 

Pros
[list]
[*]A menu format that isn't a mess (Looking at you Battlefront 2) 
[*]Unique battlefield designs that feel alive (Sarlacc Pit on Tatooine)
[*]Usage of interesting NPC combatants (Ewoks, Tusken Raiders, Gungans) which from my knowledge the sequel doesn't have.
[*] No Micro transactions!
[*] Two campaign modes, one taking place during Clone Wars, the other during the Galactic Civil War.
[*] The Galactic Conquest Gamemode, which is very fun to play. 
[*] It's worth the $10. 
[/list]

Cons
[list]
[*] Hero characters aren't playable in this game, only AI controlled. 
[*] I recommend playing on Easy mode, because changing the difficulty only makes your enemies stronger, leaving your AI team mates with the competence of a 6 year old with a bad microphone. 
[/list]
